paras: The averted lynching of Frank Brown took place at Checotah, Indian Territory, on the night of March 11, 1903, when white residents talked of lynching a Black prisoner charged with killing a white youth and Black residents armed themselves to prevent it. Deputy marshals guarded the prisoner and took him to the jail at Muskogee the next morning, after a special officer and a group of armed Black men exchanged shots in which no one was reported hurt. The killing ran as a short wire item in Texas and Kansas papers, while a Muskogee dispatch headlined "Officers Prevent Lynching" described the standoff.

According to a Checotah dispatch of March 11, a posse brought into town a Black man, printed as "Frank Dawn," charged with killing Charlie Scott, the 17-year-old son of J. D. Scott, twelve miles west of Checotah. The dispatch said the trouble was "said to have arisen" over $1.05 that the man claimed Scott owed him for picking cotton, that Scott threatened him and was turning to leave when he allegedly fired, and that a second shot broke the father's arm. It described him as a one-armed man "shipped from Dallas last fall to pick cotton." A Muskogee report the next day named him Frank Brown, called the shooting a fight, named the wounded father Ben Scott, and stated that the Scotts were white.

Once it became known that Brown, then held in the Checotah jail, had been charged, "the whites began to talk of lynching him," according to the Muskogee dispatch. Black residents "immediately organized to prevent a lynching," armed themselves, and bought all the ammunition in the town. When deputy marshals arrived they placed a guard over the prisoner, and special officers patrolled the streets.

By the officers' account, a special officer ordered a group of Black men to disperse, they opened fire, and the fire was returned; one bullet passed through the officer's hat. The group scattered and no further violence was reported, and on the morning of March 12 two deputy marshals brought Brown to Muskogee and placed him in jail.
No report of an inquest into Scott's death, a trial of Brown, or arrests among those involved in the Checotah shooting was found, and no account of the episode in the Black press has been found.

The first wire account, carried as "Territory Tragedy" by the Waxahachie Daily Light and the Bryan Morning Eagle and as "A Debt Caused a Murder" by the Abilene Weekly Reflector, reported only the killing and said nothing of a lynching threat. The Daily Ardmoreite printed the fuller Checotah version on March 12 and the Muskogee dispatch the next day under the headline "Officers Prevent Lynching" and the subhead "Negroes When Ordered to Disperse Reply With Voiley of Shots." That account credited the deputies with averting both a lynching and "a riot" and gave only the officers' version of the shooting.

The Shreveport Caucasian condensed the story into a news brief that called the armed defenders "a mob of negroes." On March 26 the Montgomery Advertiser mentioned in an editorial aside "something of a race war in Checotah," in which "white, red and back [black] were somewhat mixed," repeated another paper's claim that whiskey began it, and closed with a joke that Black men "can usually be captured that way."

The Checotah wire named the accused "Frank Dawn" and the father J. D. Scott, while the Muskogee dispatch gave Frank Brown and Ben Scott. The cause also varies: the Checotah wire cited a $1.05 cotton-picking debt, the Muskogee report gave none, and the Montgomery Advertiser relayed another paper's claim that whiskey was to blame.

reader.title: Averted lynching of Frank Brown
bases: A threatened lynching of a Black prisoner held in the Checotah jail, averted when deputies guarded him and moved him to Muskogee, with an armed Black defense and an exchange of fire with a special officer (A5, A6).

No one was killed in the lynching threat: whites only 'began to talk of lynching' Brown, accused of killing Charles Scott, and he was taken safely to Muskogee (A5, A6). It is a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

The killing of Scott and Brown's arrest are reported by an independent Checotah wire (A2) and a Muskogee dispatch (A5); the lynching threat and the shooting rest mainly on the Muskogee dispatch (A5), condensed in A6, with an independent editorial allusion to shooting at Checotah (A7).

accounts.label: Checotah wire
accounts.gist: A posse brought in 'Frank Dawn', charged with killing 17-year-old Charlie Scott over a $1.05 cotton-picking debt after Scott threatened him; no mention of a lynching threat.

accounts.label: Muskogee dispatch (officers' version)
accounts.gist: Whites talked of lynching Brown; Black residents armed to prevent it; when a special officer ordered a group to disperse they fired and he returned fire; deputies averted a lynching and took Brown to Muskogee.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser editorial
accounts.gist: A 'race war' at Checotah in which 'white, red and back [black]' were 'somewhat mixed'; another paper blamed whiskey and reported a raid in which 'one negro was captured with whiskey'.

framing.detail: Texas and Kansas papers ran the Checotah wire as 'Territory Tragedy' and 'A Debt Caused a Murder', a killing story with no lynching threat.
The Daily Ardmoreite headlined 'Officers Prevent Lynching', crediting the deputies and giving the officers' account that the Black men fired first.
The Shreveport Caucasian's brief called the armed Black defenders 'a mob of negroes'.
The Montgomery Advertiser treated the affair as a sardonic aside on a 'race war' and ended with a joke about Black men being 'captured' with whiskey.

conflicts.note: The Checotah wire and its reprints use 'Dawn'; the Muskogee dispatch and the Caucasian use 'Brown'. The later Muskogee report, from where he was jailed, is probably better on the name.

versions.value: A fight west of Checotah (no cause given)

conflicts.note: All versions are from white papers; the whiskey version is secondhand and may describe a related disturbance.
